message:
fix(toolbar): a press nobody can see, and the swapchain that outlives its release

Closes two of the three surviving explanations for "target select does nothing" and
reproduces the third.

1b was filed as not-a-defect: releasing off a button correctly cancels the press, and
the log says so. But the log is not what the user gets, and photographing the button
showed the press produced no visible change at all. The pressed look required a hover,
and the hover is cleared by WM_MOUSELEAVE, which the system sends as soon as the real
pointer is reported off the bar -- and the bar summons itself under a cursor that may
be sitting still, which generates no move to set the hover in the first place. The
pressed look now follows the press: it appears on the way down, lifts when the pointer
drags off, and comes back when it returns. A button that looks identical pressed and
unpressed is indistinguishable from a dead one, which is the pair this whole
investigation has been trying to tell apart.

4 is the mouse-suppression window the touch path arms. Linking the shipped window
procedure on its own -- with recording doubles for the features it does not drive, all
named in the test -- shows that an armed gate does swallow a picker click whole: no
selection, nothing forwarded. It is a 300ms window rather than a latch, and the only
place that arms it is the touch pointer handler, so a mouse-only session cannot gate
itself. It did that swallowing in silence, so it now says so once per window and counts
what it dropped.

5 reproduces, and it is not the ordering race it was assumed to be. With the real
present path linked and a synthetic NV12 frame -- no host, no decoder, no protocol --
the picker opens and the screen keeps the frozen frame while the window's own DC holds
the picker. The swapchain is released: ready is 0 and the pointer is null. A forced
repaint, SWP_FRAMECHANGED and a resize all leave it there. So the premise recorded in
the renderer, that dropping the swapchain returns the window to GDI, does not hold
here. The boundary is exact: with no frame ever presented the picker appears, and one
presented frame is the whole difference -- which is why the symptom only ever showed up
mid-session, and why hypotheses 1 through 3 kept coming back clean. The click, the
transition and the drawing were all working.

The remedy belongs to the present path and is left alone: this is one machine, one
console session, and the options differ in cost.
